title: He bowed not (Esther 3)
hookLine: Mordecai won't bow to Haman, and Haman plots against all the Jews
carry: the city of Shushan was perplexed
tomorrow: For such a time as this (Esther 4:14)

cards: The king's gate in Shushan. King Ahasuerus has just raised a man named Haman above all the princes, with an order: when Haman passes, the king's servants bow.
So at the gate they bow, the whole row of them bending low as he walks by. Except one man, who stays standing. He's the same man who once walked past the women's court every day to ask after Esther.

teach.b: In the JPS 1917 translation: "And all the king's servants, that were in the king's gate, bowed down, and prostrated themselves before Haman; for the king had so commanded concerning him. But Mordecai bowed not down, nor prostrated himself before him."
Day after day the servants ask why he breaks the king's command. He gives no speech.

teach.h: HE TOLD THEM HE WAS A JEW.
teach.b: What the text says he told them is this: that he was a Jew. That's the only reason the book offers. Later readers supplied their own.
Some midrashic stories say Haman wore an idol, so bowing to him meant bowing to it. Others read it as Mordecai refusing to give a man the honor he owed to God alone.
The text leaves the why at the edge and puts the weight on the act. Notice the turn. Yesterday Esther kept who she was hidden.
Today Mordecai says it out loud, and it costs.

teach.h: HAMAN'S WRATH TURNS ON A PEOPLE.
teach.b: When Haman sees that Mordecai bows not, he is full of wrath. Haman thinks it beneath him to strike at Mordecai alone; he seeks to destroy all the Jews in the kingdom. Lots are cast before him, pur, to choose the day.
Then he goes to the king and describes a certain people, scattered among the provinces, whose laws are different. The king hands over his ring. Letters go out.

teach.h: THE CITY OF SHUSHAN WAS PERPLEXED.
teach.b: And the chapter ends with two pictures side by side: "the king and Haman sat down to drink; but the city of Shushan was perplexed." Haman's anger at one man who would not bend has turned on a whole people.

how: When the scroll of Esther is read on Purim, it is a custom to drown out Haman's name with noisemakers and stamping each time it is read.

o: Esther's cousin, who would not bow to Haman
the king's adviser who plotted against the Jews
the chamberlain who cared for Esther at court

games.q: he bowed not — tap the pairs.
p: the lot cast to choose a day

s: Mordecai refused only once, the first time Haman passed
the servants spoke to him daily, the text says, and he hearkened not.
lots, called pur, were cast to choose a day
the book later says the days were called Purim after the name of pur.
Haman's anger stayed aimed at Mordecai alone
he thought it beneath him to strike Mordecai alone, and sought to destroy all the Jews.

games.q: you're Mordecai at the king's gate. Haman is passing, and every servant around you is bowing low. what do you do?
games.why: 'Mordecai bowed not down, nor prostrated himself before him.' asked why, he told them he was a Jew.

practice: If you're able, stand up; if not, sit as tall as is comfortable, feet on the floor, shoulders easy, and notice what it feels like to take up your full height.

Think of one place where you bend when you'd rather stand, a joke you laugh along with, a word you swallow, and just hold it there, with no need to change it today. If you pray, you can pray standing.

wordCard.voice: Mordecai. He stays standing when everyone at the king's gate bows to Haman, and says only that he was a Jew. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew of Esther 3:2: he would not kneel, and would not bow down.

carryVoice: Your line: the city of Shushan was perplexed. The powerful drink; the city is bewildered. That's day eight hundred sixty-six.
